analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal student loans of borrowers defrauded by colleges through false job placement or employment promises.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it sat in the Senate education committee from May 2020 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ordered the Education Department to erase the federal student loans of three groups of borrowers within 30 days: borrowers the department already found were misled about job placement rates, borrowers whose cases were filed by a state attorney general, and borrowers the department determined were promised guaranteed jobs or credit transfers that never materialized. It would have reimbursed money borrowers already paid, erased the bad credit history from those loans, and told borrowers they could apply for financial aid again. It would also have started proceedings to make the colleges that did the misleading repay the department.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers who were defrauded by their colleges and are still carrying the debt — specifically people covered by existing Education Department findings of job placement misrepresentation, borrowers whose claims were asserted by a state attorney general, and borrowers who applied for relief after a department finding of false job or credit-transfer promises. Parent borrowers who took loans for their children are covered too.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Education Department to fully discharge eligible loans, including interest, costs, and fees, within 30 days of enactment for borrowers covered by existing misrepresentation findings or state attorney general claims, whether or not their individual claims had been decided.
Reimburses borrowers within 45 days for any payments they already made toward the discharged loan, voluntarily or through enforced collection.

Requires the department to report the discharge to consumer reporting agencies within 60 days so all adverse credit history from the loan is deleted, and to stop treating defaulted borrowers as in default on the discharged loan.
Requires written notice within 20 days telling borrowers what relief they will get and that they remain eligible for federal financial aid after receiving it.

Requires the department to initiate a proceeding to make the college whose conduct caused the discharge repay the government the amount discharged, whether by offset, letter of credit, or other protection.

analysis.who_pays: The Education Department pays upfront for the discharged loans and reimbursements — in practice the federal Treasury. The bill then seeks repayment from the colleges whose misrepresentation caused the discharge, so colleges found to have misled students, particularly ones with thin finances, would bear the cost when they can pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers first, then the colleges at fault

drawbacks.text: Discharges would be automatic for broad groups based on findings against whole institutions, without individual review of each borrower's claim, which raises the cost to taxpayers if the department later pursued more borrowers than it would have approved case by case.
If the colleges that caused the discharges are insolvent or shut down, the government may never recoup the discharged amounts, leaving taxpayers with the bill.
Requiring colleges to repay discharges could push struggling institutions closer to closure, which can strand current students mid-program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the borrowers covered — people already found to have been misled about jobs or credits — full cancellation, refunds, and credit cleanup are substantial, direct relief. The main cost is fiscal: the government pays first and only recovers from colleges to the extent they can pay. The bill narrows eligibility to borrowers tied to existing department findings or state attorney general claims, which limits the exposure but also means some defrauded borrowers outside those categories would get nothing.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate education committee in May 2020, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended, so it died without any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Durbin introduced the bill on May 14, 2020, joined by Sens. Sherrod Brown and Elizabeth Warren.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day.
Ten senators cosponsored the bill, nine Democrats and one Independent.
No further action was taken; the bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no hearing record in the provided history before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defrauded borrowers got no relief from this bill, so the colleges whose misrepresentation the bill targeted avoided a requirement to repay the government for discharged loans, and taxpayers avoided the upfront cost — but only because the relief never happened, not because the need went away.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges facing repayment avoided the requirement

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no opposition positions are on the record; the sponsor and all ten cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent, and the bill went nowhere in a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: For-profit and other colleges found to have misled students
industries.note: The bill would have required these institutions to repay the government for loans discharged because of their misrepresentation about job placement, guaranteed employment, or credit transfer. Their interest in blocking it ran against borrowers seeking relief from debts caused by that misrepresentation.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and debt collectors
industries.note: Loans discharged under the bill — including defaulted ones, with payments refunded — would have removed servicing and collection revenue on those loans. Their business depends on the volume of loans in repayment.

The bill would have required deletion of adverse credit history tied to discharged loans, removing some data from their files. The effect on the bureaus is modest, while borrowers would see the negative marks erased.
